subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Infectious disease is the clinical presentation of a pathogen that disrupts host homeostasis. Diagnosis hinges on matching signs, epidemiology and targeted tests, then treating the organism and supporting the host.

sections.p: Infectious disease is a clinical syndrome caused by a pathogen that interferes with normal physiology. Clinicians must identify the organism, its mode of spread, and the host response to guide therapy.
b: Pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, prions

sections.p: Each pathogen has unique virulence factors that determine tissue tropism and immune evasion. Recognizing these helps predict complications and guide empiric therapy.
b: Fungi: cell wall components, biofilm formation

sections.p: Understanding how a pathogen moves from host to host and its life cycle stages is essential for interrupting spread and selecting effective drugs.
Clinical syndromes vary from mild self-limited infections to fulminant sepsis. Severity is staged by organ dysfunction and systemic response.
Diagnosis integrates history, physical exam, epidemiology and targeted investigations. When tests are unavailable, clinical algorithms guide empiric treatment.

t.b: Detects bacteremia; a positive result confirms invasive bacterial infection and guides antibiotic choice.
Identifies viral pathogens rapidly; a positive result confirms viral etiology and informs antiviral therapy.
Detects recent or past infection; a rising IgG titer indicates recent exposure.
Provides quick detection of common pathogens (e.g., influenza, RSV); a positive result supports early antiviral use.
Visualizes organisms (e.g., malaria parasites, cryptococcal capsule); a positive finding directs specific treatment.

sections.p: Treat the pathogen, support organ function, and prevent spread. Drug choice depends on organism, resistance patterns, and host factors.
b: Supportive care: fluids, vasopressors, organ support

sections.p: Remember that clinical context dictates the choice of tests and empiric therapy. Always consider the most likely pathogen given the epidemiology and host risk factors.
b: Vaccination status can alter disease presentation and diagnostic thresholds.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe sepsis or septic shock, sudden respiratory distress, altered mental status, uncontrolled bleeding, high fever with rash and hypotension, sudden severe pain indicating possible embolic event

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a suspected septic patient?
faq.a: Start broad‑spectrum empiric antibiotics and obtain cultures before giving antibiotics.

faq.q: Why is vaccination important in infectious disease control?
faq.a: Vaccines prevent disease, reduce transmission, and lower the need for antibiotics, limiting resistance.

faq.q: When can I rely on a negative rapid test?
faq.a: Only if the clinical suspicion is low; a negative test does not rule out infection in high‑risk patients.

exam: Explain how the qSOFA score helps identify patients at risk of sepsis.
Describe the diagnostic criteria for malaria in a patient from an endemic area.
Outline the empiric antibiotic regimen for community‑acquired pneumonia in a low‑resource setting.
